output.title: Show HN: depsentry – behavioral dependency scanner that catches supply-chain attacks before CVE disclosure
output.body:
depsentry watches what your dependencies do, not just what CVE databases say about them.

Most scanners (Snyk, Dependabot, Socket) are disclosure-driven: they alert after a CVE is filed. Supply-chain attacks like event-stream lived in an install script and a hijacked maintainer account for weeks before any CVE existed. We wanted something that catches the behavioral signals instead.

What it flags:
- New or changed install scripts (preinstall/postinstall)
- Sudden maintainer handoffs on packages you depend on
- Typosquat-adjacent package names in your lockfile
- Obfuscated payloads or new outbound network calls added in minor/patch versions

How it works: a Rust scanner pulls package metadata and release diffs from npm and PyPI registries, runs heuristic and AST-based checks, and posts a PR comment on the exact change that introduced the risk. It runs as a GitHub Action.

Retro-test: we ran it against the event-stream/flatmap-stream incident timeline and it would have flagged the malicious version 11 days before public disclosure. That's a specific, falsifiable claim — happy to share the methodology.

Perf: 1,200-dependency lockfile scans in ~40 seconds in CI.

Current state: public beta, free for open-source repos (running on ~300 public projects now), $199/month team plan.

Known gaps: no GitLab support yet, Python coverage is newer and less battle-tested than npm, no independent benchmark against competitors.

Looking for feedback on the detection heuristics, false-positive rate in real codebases, and whether the PR-comment UX is actually useful or just noise. {APP_URL}
warnings: The retro-test claim (11 days before disclosure) is specific and should be verifiable — be prepared for HN to ask for the methodology and raw data; have it ready to share in comments.
'~300 public projects' is a soft number — if HN asks for precision, clarify it's approximate.
Do not overstate detection completeness vs. Socket; the profile explicitly notes no independent benchmark exists.
HN will likely ask about false-positive rates — have real data ready or acknowledge you don't yet have a published benchmark.
